Containers on AWS: Amazon ECS, AWS Fargate, Amazon EKS, and Amazon ECR

Run containers on AWS: store images in Amazon ECR, orchestrate them with Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS, and run them on Amazon EC2 or AWS Fargate.

Overview and Objectives

Lesson Overview

Serverless, Integration, and Event-Driven Design

Module 273, Serverless, Integration, and Event-Driven Design, covers serverless compute, application integration, and event-driven architectures on AWS. This lesson covers containers, with AWS Fargate as the serverless way to run them.

Containers package an application so that it runs the same way everywhere. This lesson explains how Amazon ECR stores the images, how Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS orchestrate the containers, and how Amazon EC2 or AWS Fargate runs them, with the roles, networking, storage, and scaling that production needs. You then learn to choose a platform. The last two tabs prepare you for the AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03) exam.

In this lesson, we will focus on the containers part of the AWS compute choices. AWS offers three ways to run code: virtual machines with Amazon EC2, containers, and functions with AWS Lambda. Containers use an orchestrator, Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS, and a data plane that runs them, either Amazon EC2 instances that you manage or AWS Fargate, which is serverless.

In this lesson, we will:

  • Store container images in Amazon ECR.
  • Orchestrate containers with Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS.
  • Run containers on Amazon EC2 instances that you manage, or on serverless AWS Fargate.
  • Choose between containers and AWS Lambda functions for a workload.

The tabs in this lesson cover the following topics:

  • Tab 1: why containers, an overview of Docker, how containers and images work, a hands-on Docker exercise, virtual machines, and container orchestration on AWS.
  • Tab 2: storing, scanning, and managing images in Amazon ECR.
  • Tab 3: clusters, task definitions, tasks, services, standalone tasks, and deployments.
  • Tab 4: the EC2 and Fargate launch types, Fargate Spot, and capacity providers.
  • Tab 5: IAM roles, networking and load balancing, storage, scaling, and common ECS architecture patterns.
  • Tab 6: managed Kubernetes, node types, permissions, storage, load balancing, and running containers on premises.
  • Tab 7: choosing between Lambda, ECS, and EKS, App Runner and ECS Express Mode, and pricing.
  • Tab 8: the SAA-C03 cheat sheet, exam scenarios, and the lesson summary.
  • Tab 9: open-ended Knowledge Check questions with model answers.

Introduction

Lambda runs short functions without servers, but many applications are long-running services packaged as containers. AWS offers two container orchestrators and two ways to supply the compute, and exam questions often ask which combination fits a scenario, and which IAM role or storage option a container needs.

This lesson follows FlashCart Inc. through the Problem Statement of each tab. It assumes Lessons 273.1 to 273.4, and Amazon EC2, Elastic Load Balancing, and Auto Scaling from Module 270.

Use the tab list on the left, or the Previous and Next buttons, to move through the lesson. Each topic tab opens with a Problem Statement and ends with exam traps, keyword triggers, and resource links. The Knowledge Check is the last tab.

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to:

  1. Define containers and identify the roles of Amazon ECR, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, Amazon EC2, and AWS Fargate.
  2. Use Amazon ECR to store, scan, and manage container images.
  3. Implement an ECS service and standalone tasks from a task definition.
  4. Apply IAM roles, networking, load balancing, storage, and scaling to ECS workloads.
  5. Distinguish the EC2 and Fargate launch types, and select the compute, including Fargate Spot and capacity providers, for a workload.
  6. Evaluate Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Lambda, and ECS Express Mode for a workload, and justify the choice.
  7. Design a secure, scalable container architecture on AWS.

1. Containers and Orchestration

Problem Statement

FlashCart runs its product catalog and search services on four EC2 servers in one data center. Each server was installed by hand, with a slightly different version of Java and of the libraries. A release that works on a developer laptop often fails on one of the servers, and setting up a new server takes two days.

The engineering team wants to package each service with everything it needs, so that it runs the same way on a laptop, in testing, and in production. The team also wants a system that starts the services on the right servers, restarts them when they fail, and adds copies when the traffic grows, instead of a person doing it by hand.

Your challenge:

  • Explain how containers solve the "works on my laptop" problem, and how they differ from virtual machines.
  • Explain what a container orchestrator does, and the difference between its control plane and its data plane.
  • Name the AWS services that provide each part.

1.1 Why Containers

  • An application needs more than its code: it also needs libraries, dependencies, and configuration. When the server has a different version of a library than the developer’s workstation, for example OpenSSL 3.1.0 instead of 3.2.0, the application can fail after it is pushed.
  • A container packages the application together with its code, libraries, dependencies, and configuration, so it runs the same way on a laptop, a server, a virtual machine, or the cloud.
  • A container is lightweight virtualization: it runs an application and its dependencies in a resource-isolated process.
BenefitWhat it means
IsolatedEach container has its own filesystem, process space, and network environment.
LightweightNo full operating system to carry, so containers are small and start fast.
ConsistentThe container holds all its dependencies, so it is the same everywhere.
PortableIt is easy to package, ship, and run on any platform: a local machine, a server, or the cloud.

1.2 How Containers Work

1.2.1 Overview of Docker

  • Docker is an open platform for developing, shipping, and running applications in containers. It is the best-known container tool, and most container workflows start with it.
  • Docker uses a client-server architecture: the Docker client sends commands to the Docker daemon, which does the work.
PartWhat it does
Docker client (docker CLI)The command-line tool that you use, for example docker build or docker run. It sends each command to the daemon.
Docker daemon (dockerd)The background service on the host that builds images and runs and manages containers, networks, and volumes.
Docker EngineThe daemon, its API, and the client together. Under the engine, a lower-level runtime, containerd, starts the containers.
Docker DesktopAn application that runs Docker on Windows and macOS laptops.
RegistryStores images, for example Docker Hub, the default public registry, or Amazon ECR (tab 2).
  • Docker manages four kinds of objects: images (read-only templates), containers (running images), networks (how containers talk to each other), and volumes (data that outlives a container).
  • Docker Compose defines and runs an application of several containers, such as a web container and a database container, from one YAML file.
  • Docker images follow the Open Container Initiative (OCI) standard, so an image built with Docker runs on any OCI-compatible runtime, including Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, and AWS Fargate.
CommandWhat it does
docker build -t myapp .Builds an image named myapp from the Dockerfile in the current folder.
docker imagesLists the images on the host.
docker run -d -p 80:8080 myappStarts a container in the background and maps port 80 of the host to port 8080 of the container.
docker psLists the running containers.
docker logs <container>Shows the output of a container.
docker stop <container>Stops a running container.
docker push and docker pullUpload an image to a registry, or download one from it.

1.2.2 What Makes Containers Work

  • A container engine, such as Docker, containerd, CRI-O, or Podman, runs containers with three features of the Linux kernel:
  • Namespaces isolate what a container can see and access, such as its processes, network, and filesystem.
  • Control groups (cgroups) limit and monitor the CPU, memory, and I/O that a container uses.
  • A union filesystem stacks the layers of an image, so containers share common files and use disk space efficiently.

1.2.3 Container Images and the Dockerfile

  • A container image is a read-only template that holds the application and everything it needs. It is packed, repeatable, immutable, and portable. A running image is a container.
  • An image is built in layers: each instruction of the Dockerfile adds a layer. Layers are cached and shared between images, so builds are fast and images use less storage.
  • A running container adds a thin writable layer on top of the image. The changes in that layer are lost when the container is removed, so keep data in volumes or in services such as Amazon EFS or Amazon S3.
  • A Dockerfile is a text file with the instructions to build an image.
InstructionWhat it does
FROMSets the base image to start from, such as python:3.12-slim.
WORKDIRSets the working folder inside the image.
COPYCopies files from your computer into the image.
RUNRuns a command while the image is built, for example to install libraries.
ENVSets an environment variable.
EXPOSEDocuments the port that the application listens on.
CMD or ENTRYPOINTSets the command that runs when a container starts.

Example of a Dockerfile:

FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["python", "app.py"]

This Dockerfile starts from a small Python base image, installs the libraries of the application, copies the code, and starts the application on port 8080. The build command creates the image, and you push it to a registry so that any server or AWS service can pull and run it.

Try It: Run a Docker Container on an EC2 Instance

Run a simple web server in a Docker container on an Amazon Linux EC2 instance. The security group of the instance must allow inbound HTTP (port 80) from your IP address, and the instance needs internet access to download the httpd base image from Docker Hub.

  1. Install the Docker engine: sudo yum install docker -y.
  2. Start the Docker daemon: sudo service docker start.
  3. Create a sample index.html file in a new folder.
  4. In the same folder, create a file named Dockerfile with these two lines:
FROM httpd
COPY index.html /usr/local/apache2/htdocs/
  1. Build the image with sudo docker build -t mywebserver ., where the final dot means the current folder.
  2. Run the container: sudo docker run --name my-web-server -p 80:80 -d mywebserver.
  3. Open the public IP address of the EC2 instance in a browser, and check that your page appears.
  4. Clean up: stop the container with sudo docker stop my-web-server, and terminate the instance when you are done.

1.3 Containers and Virtual Machines

Virtual machinesContainers
What is sharedEach VM has its own guest operating system on a hypervisor.Containers share the host operating system kernel.
Size and start timeGigabytes, and minutes to start.Megabytes, and seconds to start.
DensityA few VMs per server.Many containers per server.
IsolationStrong, at the hardware level.Process-level isolation, which is lighter.

1.4 Why Containers Need Orchestration

  • A monolith runs the user interface, the business logic, and the data access as one application.
  • Teams often split it into microservices, such as order, billing and payment, search, product catalog, and email, each running in many containers.
  • Running hundreds of containers by hand is not possible, so a container orchestrator handles: scheduling and placement, resource allocation, health checks and restarts, creating and exposing services, network communication, monitoring, logging, and authentication and authorization.
  • Open-source orchestrators include Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, Apache Mesos, and OpenShift. Kubernetes is the most widely used, and cloud providers offer it as a managed service, such as Amazon EKS.

1.5 Docker Containers Management on AWS

  • The control plane of the orchestrator decides where containers run and keeps them running. On AWS, it is Amazon ECS, the AWS container orchestrator, or Amazon EKS, managed Kubernetes.
  • The data plane is the compute that runs the containers: Amazon EC2 instances that you manage, or AWS Fargate, serverless compute where AWS manages the servers.
  • Amazon ECR stores the images.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A team wants its application to run the same way on laptops, in testing, and in production, and to start in seconds, with many copies per server. What should a solutions architect recommend?

  • A. Use a larger EC2 instance type.
  • B. Create a separate virtual machine image for each environment.
  • C. Install the application by hand on each server.
  • D. Package the application as a container image.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: D. A container image packages the application with its dependencies, starts in seconds, and many containers can share one server.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectA bigger server does not make releases consistent.
BIncorrectSeparate images drift apart, and VMs are larger and slower to start.
CIncorrectManual installs cause the differences between servers.
DCorrectContainers are portable, fast to start, and dense.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Control plane = ECS or EKS. Data plane = EC2 or Fargate. Image registry = ECR.
  • Containers share the host kernel; VMs each have a guest operating system.
  • Container isolation comes from namespaces, and resource limits from control groups.

Memory Hook

ECR stores the box, ECS or EKS decides where it goes, EC2 or Fargate runs it.

Trigger 2: "Build an image with instructions in a text file"

→ AWS Fargate

2. Amazon ECR

Problem Statement

FlashCart’s images are now built automatically, but they are stored on Docker Hub under a developer’s personal account. The security team is worried: anyone could change an image, nobody checks the images for known vulnerabilities, and the company cannot control who downloads them.

There are other problems too. The build system creates about 50 new images a day, and old images are never deleted. The team in a second Region pulls every image across the ocean, which is slow. A rule from the auditors says that a released image with the tag "v1.4.2" must never be overwritten by a different image with the same tag.

Your challenge:

  • Choose where to store the images, and how to control who can push and pull them.
  • Find known vulnerabilities in the images automatically.
  • Remove old images automatically, and serve the images close to the second Region.
  • Stop a released tag from being overwritten.

2.1 What Amazon ECR Is

  • Use ECR to store and manage Docker images on AWS.
  • Amazon Elastic Container Registry (ECR) is a fully managed registry for container images.
  • Repositories are private by default. ECR also offers public repositories, through the Amazon ECR Public Gallery.
  • Access is controlled with IAM policies and repository policies, for example to let another account pull images.
  • A permission error when you push or pull an image usually points to an IAM or repository policy.
  • ECR is integrated with ECS and EKS: tasks and pods pull their images from ECR with their IAM roles.
  • ECR is fully integrated with ECS, and it is backed by Amazon S3.
  • Each image version is identified by a tag, such as v1.4.2 or latest, and by an immutable digest, a hash of the image content.
  • Images are encrypted in transit and at rest, and you can use an AWS KMS key.
  • ECR supports image vulnerability scanning, versioning, image tags, and image lifecycle policies (section 2.2).

2.2 Key Features

FeatureWhat it does
Image scanningFinds known vulnerabilities. Basic scanning runs on push. Enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector and scans continuously.
Lifecycle policiesDelete images automatically by rule, for example keep only the last 30 images, or remove untagged images after 14 days.
Tag immutabilityStops a tag, such as v1.4.2, from being overwritten by a different image.
ReplicationCopies images automatically to other Regions or other accounts.
Pull through cacheCaches images from upstream public registries in your private ECR registry.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: An auditor requires that a released image tag can never point to a different image, and the security team wants every image checked for known vulnerabilities continuously. Which ECR features meet both needs?

  • A. Tag immutability and enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector.
  • B. Lifecycle policies and replication.
  • C. A public repository and basic scanning.
  • D. Repository policies and pull through cache.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: A. Tag immutability prevents overwriting a tag, and enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector to scan images continuously.

OptionResultReason
ACorrectEach feature meets one of the needs.
BIncorrectThese remove and copy images.
CIncorrectA public repository exposes the images.
DIncorrectThese control access and caching.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Store and scan images on AWS = ECR. Continuous vulnerability scanning = enhanced scanning with Amazon Inspector.
  • Clean up old images = lifecycle policy. Other Regions or accounts = replication.

Memory Hook

ECR stores, scans, cleans, locks, and copies your images.

SAA-C03 Keyword Triggers

Trigger 1: "Private registry for container images on AWS"
→ Amazon ECR

Trigger 2: "Delete old images automatically"
→ ECR lifecycle policy

Trigger 3: "Prevent a tag from being overwritten"
→ Tag immutability

Trigger 4: "Images close to another Region"
→ ECR replication

  • Docs Scan images for software vulnerabilities in Amazon ECR

3. Amazon ECS Concepts

Problem Statement

FlashCart decides to run its catalog service on Amazon ECS. The service has two containers: the web API and a small agent that ships logs. It must always have three copies running behind a load balancer, and a failed copy must be replaced automatically. A new version must roll out without downtime.

The team also has a nightly job that rebuilds the search index. It runs for about 40 minutes and then stops, and it should not keep any compute running during the day.

Your challenge:

  • Describe how ECS describes the catalog service, and how it keeps three copies running.
  • Explain how to run the nightly index job, which must start, run, and stop.
  • Explain how a new version rolls out without downtime.

3.1 What Amazon ECS Is

  • Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) is a fully managed container orchestration service that deploys, manages, and scales containerized applications.
  • It integrates with AWS tools, such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and with third-party tools, such as Docker, so teams can focus on building applications instead of the environment.
  • You can run and scale container workloads across AWS Regions in the cloud and on premises, without managing a control plane.
  • It lets you run, stop, and manage Docker containers on a cluster of EC2 instances that you manage, including Spot Instances, or on Fargate serverless compute, where AWS manages the infrastructure (tab 4).
  • ECS handles these tasks for you:
    • Scheduling containers on available compute resources.
    • Managing the container lifecycle: start, stop, and restart.
    • Balancing load across tasks.
    • Scaling tasks and capacity.
    • Monitoring task health.
    • Handling networking.
  • ECS integrates with many AWS services:
    • Application Load Balancer and Network Load Balancer (as application backend services).
    • Amazon API Gateway (as an API backend service).
    • Amazon EventBridge (for event-based execution).
    • Amazon CloudWatch (for metrics and logs).
    • AWS IAM (for roles and permissions).
    • Application Auto Scaling and EC2 Auto Scaling groups (for scaling tasks and instances).
  • ECS is a good choice when you want a simpler, AWS-native container service with minimal operational overhead.

3.1.1 Three Layers of Amazon ECS

Amazon ECS has three layers:

  • Capacity: the infrastructure where your containers run.
  • Controller: the Amazon ECS scheduler, the software that deploys and manages your applications.
  • Provisioning: the tools that you use to talk to the scheduler to deploy and manage your applications and containers.

The following diagram shows the Amazon ECS layers.

3.1.2 Capacity Options

Capacity optionWho manages the infrastructureNotes
Amazon ECS Managed InstancesAWS provisions, patches, scales, and maintains the underlying instances.Runs on a range of EC2 instance types, so you can use GPU acceleration, specific CPU architectures, high network performance, or specialized instance types.
Amazon EC2 instancesYou choose the instance type and the number of instances, and you manage the capacity.Runs in the AWS Cloud.
AWS FargateAWS. You do not manage servers, plan capacity, or isolate container workloads for security.Serverless and pay as you go, in the AWS Cloud.
Amazon ECS AnywhereYou manage the on-premises server or virtual machine (VM).Registers an external instance, such as an on-premises server or VM, to your ECS cluster.

ECS pricing depends on the capacity option that you choose. Check the Amazon ECS pricing page and the AWS Fargate pricing page for current prices (section 7.3).

3.1.3 Scaling and Account Features

  • Cluster Auto Scaling: ECS manages the scaling of the EC2 instances that are registered to your cluster.
  • Service Auto Scaling: ECS increases or decreases the desired number of tasks in your service automatically (section 5.4).
  • Account setting: an ECS account setting allows access to features.

3.1.4 Provisioning Options

ToolWhat it does
AWS Management ConsoleProvides a web interface to access your ECS resources.
AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI)Provides commands for a broad set of AWS services, including ECS, on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
AWS SDKsProvide language-specific APIs and handle connection details such as signing requests, retrying requests, and handling errors.
AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK)Models and provisions your application resources using familiar programming languages, in a safe and repeatable way, through AWS CloudFormation.

3.1.5 Services Used with Amazon ECS

ServiceRole with ECS
Amazon EC2 Auto ScalingKeeps the correct number of EC2 instances available to handle the load.
Amazon CloudWatchMonitors your services and tasks.
Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR)Stores and manages container images.
Elastic Load BalancingDistributes incoming service traffic automatically.
Amazon GuardDutyDetects potentially unauthorized or malicious use of your container instances and workloads.

3.2 ECS Building Blocks

ConceptWhat it is
ClusterA logical group of tasks and services, and of the capacity that runs them.
Task definitionA JSON blueprint for one or more containers: the images, CPU and memory, ports, environment variables, IAM roles, network mode, and logging.
TaskA running instance of a task definition, with one or more containers that run together.
ServiceKeeps a desired number of tasks running, replaces failed tasks, registers them with a load balancer, and rolls out new versions.
Standalone taskA task that you run once, for example a batch job. EventBridge can run tasks on a schedule or on an event.

This task definition, from the course slides, runs one nginx container on Fargate, with 0.25 vCPU, 512 MB of memory, and a task role that can read from S3:

{
  "family": "sample-task",
  "networkMode": "awsvpc",
  "requiresCompatibilities": ["FARGATE"],
  "cpu": "256",
  "memory": "512",
  "taskRoleArn": "arn:aws:iam::112233445566:role/S3ReadTaskRole",
  "containerDefinitions": [
    {
      "name": "app",
      "image": "nginx:latest",
      "essential": true,
      "portMappings": [ { "containerPort": 80 } ]
    }
  ]
}

3.3 Deployments

  • A rolling update replaces the tasks of a service a few at a time, while the load balancer sends traffic only to healthy tasks.
  • A blue/green deployment starts the new version next to the old one and then shifts the traffic, so you can roll back quickly.
  • There is no extra charge for ECS itself: you pay for the compute that runs the tasks.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A company must run a container job every night that processes files for about 40 minutes and then stops, with no compute running during the day. Which ECS approach fits best?

  • A. A Lambda function with the maximum timeout.
  • B. An ECS service with a desired count of 1 that runs all day.
  • C. An EventBridge schedule that runs a standalone ECS task on Fargate.
  • D. An EC2 instance that runs the container all day.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. A scheduled standalone task starts, runs to completion, and stops, and Fargate charges only while it runs.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectLambda stops after 15 minutes.
BIncorrectA service keeps the task running all day.
CCorrectIt runs only when needed, without servers.
DIncorrectThe instance costs money all day.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • Task definition = blueprint. Task = running copy. Service = keeps N tasks running behind a load balancer.
  • Batch or scheduled container work = a standalone task, started by EventBridge.

Memory Hook

Define the task, run the task, and let the service keep it running.

4. ECS Launch Types

Problem Statement

The catalog service runs on ECS, and the team now argues about the compute underneath. The operations engineer manages EC2 instances today and spends hours each month on patching and on resizing the instances, which are 30 percent used most of the day.

The search team has a different need: one service needs GPU instances for a ranking model, and runs at a steady, predictable load all year. The data team runs batch jobs that can be stopped and restarted at any time, and it wants them to be as cheap as possible.

Your challenge:

  • Compare the EC2 and Fargate launch types: what you manage, how you pay, and what each one allows.
  • Choose the compute for the catalog service, the GPU ranking service, and the interruptible batch jobs.
  • Explain how capacity providers mix regular and Spot capacity.

4.1 AWS Fargate Overview

  • AWS Fargate is serverless compute for running containers on AWS.
  • It runs Docker containers on AWS-managed infrastructure, so there are no EC2 instances to manage.
  • You define the container image, the CPU, and the memory, and Fargate runs the containers.
  • Pricing is pay-as-you-go.
  • Fargate works with Amazon ECS tasks and Amazon EKS pods.
  • Fargate always uses the awsvpc network mode: each task behaves like a first-class VPC resource, with its own elastic network interface (ENI) and security groups.
  • You can monitor Fargate workloads with CloudWatch Container Insights.
  • Section 4.2 compares Fargate with the EC2 launch type that you already know.

4.2 ECS Launch Types

EC2 launch typeFargate launch type
ServersYou provision and maintain the EC2 instances, which run the ECS agent and register to the cluster.No instances to manage. AWS runs each task on its own isolated compute.
SizingYou choose instance types, including GPU and special instances, and pack tasks onto them.You choose CPU and memory per task, from 0.25 vCPU up to 16 vCPU and 120 GB of memory.
PricingYou pay for the instances, whether the tasks use them fully or not. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans apply.You pay per second for the vCPU, memory, and storage that each task requests. Compute Savings Plans apply.
Networkingawsvpc, bridge, or host network mode.Always awsvpc: each task gets its own elastic network interface.
Best forSpecial hardware, full control of the host, and steady, high utilization.Most services and jobs, when you do not want to manage servers.
  • AWS also lists Amazon ECS Managed Instances as a third ECS compute option, in which AWS provisions and manages the EC2 instances that run your tasks. Check the ECS documentation for its current features.

4.2.1 ECS on the Fargate Launch Type

  • AWS Fargate is a serverless way to host Amazon ECS workloads.
  • With the Fargate launch type, you run containerized applications without provisioning and managing the underlying infrastructure.

4.2.2 ECS on the EC2 Launch Type

  • ECS makes many aspects of container and cluster management easier, but not all of them.
  • With the EC2 launch type, you register your ECS clusters and run containerized applications on EC2 instances that you manage yourself.
  • You keep control of the infrastructure, but you must provision, scale, and monitor the EC2 instances.

4.2.3 Amazon ECS Anywhere: Running Containers at an On-Premises Location

  • Amazon ECS Anywhere is an ECS feature that makes it easier to run and manage container workloads on customer-managed infrastructure.
  • It extends the simplicity of ECS to your on-premises data center, with a consistent API and tooling experience for container applications in the cloud and on premises.
  • It provides the same cluster monitoring, management, and workload scheduling as ECS in the cloud.
  • ECS Anywhere supports registering an external instance, such as an on-premises server or virtual machine (VM), to your Amazon ECS cluster.
  • The ECS control plane stays in AWS, and an agent runs on your servers.

4.3 More About Fargate

  • Each Fargate task gets 20 GiB of ephemeral storage by default, which you can raise up to 200 GiB.
  • Fargate Spot runs interruptible tasks on spare capacity at a lower price. AWS can stop a Spot task with a two-minute warning, so use it for fault-tolerant work.
  • Fargate supports the arm64 (Graviton) architecture, for a better price and performance on many workloads.
  • Fargate also runs Kubernetes pods for Amazon EKS (tab 6).

4.4 Capacity Providers

  • A capacity provider tells ECS where to run tasks: FARGATE, FARGATE_SPOT, or an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances, which ECS can scale with managed scaling.
  • A capacity provider strategy mixes them with a base and weights. For example, run the first 2 tasks on Fargate, and then 3 tasks on Fargate Spot for every 1 on Fargate.
  • ECS Anywhere also lets you register your own on-premises servers as external instances in an ECS cluster.

4.5 Amazon ECS Pricing and Costs

  • There is no additional charge for Amazon ECS itself. You pay only for the AWS resources that you create to store and run your applications.
  • There are no minimum fees or upfront obligations.

4.5.1 Drawbacks of the EC2 Launch Type

  • You must define which instance type to use and when to scale up.
  • You are responsible for configuring, monitoring, maintaining, patching, and securing the underlying EC2 instances.
  • Instance size is fixed, so you must know your container requirements in advance and avoid instances that are too large or too small.

4.5.2 Advantages of the EC2 Launch Type

  • You have more control to tailor the infrastructure to your requirements, such as choosing GPU-optimized or network-optimized instances.
  • For current instance prices, check the Amazon EC2 pricing page.

5. ECS Security, Networking, Storage, and Scaling

Problem Statement

The catalog service is moving to production, and four teams have requirements. The security team wants each service to have only the permissions it needs: the catalog reads one DynamoDB table, and the image service writes to one S3 bucket. Database passwords must not appear in the task definition.

The web team needs one load balancer in front of the catalog and search services, with each path, /catalog and /search, going to the right service. The content team needs several tasks in different Availability Zones to share the same uploaded files. The operations team wants the number of tasks to follow the traffic: three at night and up to 30 during a sale, and a separate order service to scale with the length of its SQS queue.

Your challenge:

  • Give each service its own permissions, and keep the passwords out of the task definition.
  • Put one load balancer in front of both services, with path-based routing.
  • Give tasks in several Availability Zones a shared, persistent file system.
  • Scale the catalog service with the traffic, and the order service with its queue.
  • ECS security: ECS integrates with AWS IAM, VPC, and AWS KMS, so your workloads remain secure and isolated.
  • Sections 5.1 and 5.2 cover IAM roles and VPC networking for ECS tasks.

5.1 IAM Roles for ECS

RoleUsed byWhat it allows
Container instance role (EC2 launch type)The ECS agent on each EC2 instance.Registering the instance with the cluster and making ECS API calls.
Task execution roleECS, on behalf of the task.Pulling images from ECR, sending container logs to CloudWatch Logs, and reading secrets from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store.
Task roleThe application code in the containers.Calling AWS services, such as reading a DynamoDB table or writing to an S3 bucket. Each task definition can have its own role.
  • Store passwords in AWS Secrets Manager or Systems Manager Parameter Store, and reference them in the task definition. ECS injects them as environment variables when the task starts.

Source Note

One course slide lists two ECS roles: the EC2 instance profile and the task role. It describes the image pulls, logs, and secrets as work of the instance profile. That is true for the ECS agent on the EC2 launch type, but ECS also uses a separate task execution role for these actions, and Fargate tasks always rely on it. This lesson uses all three roles.

5.2 Amazon ECS: Load Balancer Integrations

  • In awsvpc mode, each task gets its own elastic network interface and private IP address, so you can attach security groups to each task.
  • An Application Load Balancer works for most services. It routes by path or host name, such as /catalog and /search, to different services, and it supports dynamic port mapping on EC2.
  • A Network Load Balancer is recommended for very high throughput, TCP and UDP traffic, or AWS PrivateLink.
  • ECS Service Connect lets services find and call each other by name inside the cluster.

5.3 Amazon ECS: Data Volumes With Amazon Elastic File System

  • Task storage is ephemeral: it is lost when the task stops.
  • Amazon EFS gives persistent, shared storage that tasks in any Availability Zone can mount at the same time, with both the EC2 and Fargate launch types. Fargate with EFS is a fully serverless design.
  • Amazon EFS provides a managed Linux file system that multiple tasks can mount. It is supported on both ECS on EC2 and ECS on Fargate.
  • You mount EFS volumes through the ECS task definition.
  • Fargate + EFS = Serverless: Fargate runs the tasks and EFS stores the data, so you manage no servers for compute or storage.
  • Amazon EBS volumes can also be attached to tasks, for storage that one task uses.

5.4 ECS Service Auto Scaling

  • ECS Service Auto Scaling changes the desired number of tasks with AWS Application Auto Scaling, using the CPU and memory metrics that ECS publishes to CloudWatch.
  • Target tracking keeps a metric steady, like a thermostat, for example the average CPU at 50 percent, or the ALB request count per target. It can use 20-second, high-resolution CPU and memory metrics to react faster.
  • Step scaling adds tasks in steps on CloudWatch alarm thresholds, for example 1 task above 40 percent CPU and 2 tasks above 60 percent.
  • Scheduled scaling changes the capacity at set times, such as more tasks every morning and fewer at night.
  • Predictive scaling uses machine learning on historical metrics to add tasks ahead of recurring traffic peaks.
  • With the EC2 launch type, the cluster also needs enough instances: an Auto Scaling group capacity provider with managed scaling adds instances when tasks cannot be placed.
  • CloudWatch Container Insights collects metrics and logs for clusters, services, and tasks.

5.4.1 ECS Scaling: Service CPU Usage Example

5.5 ECS Common Architecture Patterns

PatternHow it works
Application backendAn Elastic Load Balancer sends traffic to several ECS services, each with its own tasks, which use a database such as DynamoDB.
API backendAmazon API Gateway sends API calls to ECS services (Lesson 273.2).
Event-driven data processingAn S3 upload sends an event to EventBridge, whose rule runs an ECS task that downloads the file, processes it, and writes the output.
Queue-based batch processingAn application sends job requests to an SQS queue. ECS tasks poll the queue, and ECS Service Auto Scaling follows the queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible) from CloudWatch (Lesson 273.3).

5.6 Amazon ECS Best Practices

  • Use Amazon ECR to store private container images.
  • Enable CloudWatch Logs to monitor your containers.
  • Apply an IAM role to each task, following the principle of least privilege.
  • Use an Application Load Balancer for service discovery and load balancing.
  • Implement Auto Scaling based on metrics.
  • Automate deployments with CI/CD, using GitHub Actions, AWS CodePipeline, or Jenkins.

5.7 Real-World Example: Deploying a Node.js API

Suppose that you deploy a Node.js API on Amazon ECS:

  1. Build the Docker image, and push it to Amazon ECR.
  2. Create an ECS task definition that uses that image.
  3. Create a Fargate service with a desired count of 2.
  4. Attach an Application Load Balancer.
  5. Let ECS manage scaling and failover automatically.

The result is a scalable, highly available API that you deploy without managing any servers.

  • B. In the task execution role.

OptionResultReason

6. Amazon EKS

Problem Statement

FlashCart is buying a smaller company, ShopLens, that runs 40 microservices on Kubernetes in its own data center. Its engineers know Kubernetes well and use Kubernetes tools every day. They do not want to rewrite their deployment files for a different orchestrator, and they want to keep the option of running some services on premises.

They do not want to operate the Kubernetes control plane themselves, as they do today, because upgrades take a week and failed twice last year. Some services need specific EC2 instance types, others have unpredictable traffic, and the team would rather not manage nodes at all if possible.

Your challenge:

  • Choose the AWS service for ShopLens, and explain why it fits better than ECS for this team.
  • Compare the ways to provide nodes: Auto Mode, managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Fargate, and Hybrid Nodes.
  • Explain how pods get AWS permissions and persistent storage.

6.1 What Amazon EKS Is

  • Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) runs managed Kubernetes clusters on AWS. Kubernetes is an open-source system for deploying, scaling, and managing containerized applications.
  • AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you, across several Availability Zones, and handles its availability and upgrades.
  • EKS runs upstream, certified conformant Kubernetes. Because it is standard Kubernetes, teams keep their Kubernetes tools and files, and workloads stay portable to other Kubernetes environments, including on premises and other clouds.
  • EKS is a good choice when a team already has experience running Kubernetes at scale in production.
  • Containers run in pods on nodes. Images usually come from ECR.

6.2 Node Types

Node typeHow it works
EKS Auto ModeAWS also manages the nodes: it provisions, scales, updates, and secures them based on the workloads.
Managed node groupsEKS creates and manages EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group for you, with On-Demand or Spot Instances.
Self-managed nodesYou create and manage the EC2 instances yourself, for full control. Spot Instances work here too.
AWS FargateServerless: each pod runs on its own isolated compute, with no nodes to manage.
EKS Hybrid NodesYour on-premises and edge servers join the EKS cluster as nodes, while AWS runs the control plane.

6.3 Permissions, Storage, and Load Balancing

  • Permissions: give pods AWS permissions with EKS Pod Identity, which AWS recommends, or with IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA), so each pod has only the permissions that it needs.
  • Storage: persistent volumes use Container Storage Interface (CSI) drivers for Amazon EBS, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx. You describe them with a StorageClass in the cluster.
  • Load balancing: the AWS Load Balancer Controller creates Application Load Balancers and Network Load Balancers for Kubernetes services.
  • Pricing: you pay for each EKS cluster per hour, plus the compute that runs the pods.

6.4 Running Containers on Premises

OptionWhere the control plane runsWho manages itUse it when
Amazon ECS AnywhereIn AWS (Amazon ECS).AWS runs ECS. You run the ECS agent and the AWS Systems Manager agent on your servers.You want ECS to manage containers on your own servers or VMs.
Amazon EKS Hybrid NodesIn AWS (Amazon EKS).AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane. Your servers join the cluster as nodes.You want one EKS cluster across AWS and your data centers.
Amazon EKS AnywhereOn your own infrastructure.You run and maintain the clusters, with AWS tools built on EKS Distro. An optional enterprise subscription adds AWS support and curated packages.The whole cluster must run on premises or at the edge, for example for regulated or disconnected sites.
  • EKS Anywhere clusters can still use AWS services such as Amazon ECR for images and CloudWatch for logs and metrics, and the EKS Connector shows them in the EKS console.

7. Choosing a Platform and Pricing

Problem Statement

FlashCart now has five teams that want to run new code, and the architecture review board must choose the platform for each one. The image team needs a function that resizes each uploaded picture in about two seconds. The catalog team runs a container service with steady traffic and does not want to manage servers. The search team runs a GPU ranking model at a constant load all year.

ShopLens brings its Kubernetes microservices. A new marketing team wants the simplest possible way to put a small containerized website online, with a load balancer, HTTPS, and scaling, and asks whether it can use AWS App Runner, as a blog post suggests. The finance team asks how each platform is billed.

Your challenge:

  • Choose the platform for each of the five teams, and justify each choice.
  • Answer the marketing team’s question about App Runner, and name the current alternative.
  • Explain how ECS, Fargate, and EKS are billed.

7.1 Choosing the Platform

NeedPlatform
Short, event-driven code with no serversAWS Lambda (Lesson 273.1)
Containers without managing serversAmazon ECS on Fargate
Containers that need GPUs, special instances, or host control, or steady high utilizationAmazon ECS with the EC2 launch type
Kubernetes, portability, or existing Kubernetes tools and skillsAmazon EKS
The simplest way to run a containerized web applicationAmazon ECS Express Mode

7.2 AWS App Runner and ECS Express Mode

  • AWS App Runner deployed web applications from source code or a container image, with load balancing, HTTPS, and scaling built in.
  • App Runner is no longer open to new customers since April 30, 2026. Existing customers can keep using it, but AWS does not plan new features. Older study material may still recommend it.
  • AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode instead. You provide a container image and two IAM roles, and ECS creates the whole application stack in your account: an ECS service on Fargate, an Application Load Balancer, auto scaling, networking, and a default URL.

7.3 Pricing

ServiceWhat you pay for
Amazon ECSNo extra charge for ECS itself. You pay for the EC2 instances or the Fargate tasks.
AWS FargateThe vCPU, memory, and extra ephemeral storage that each task or pod requests, per second. Fargate Spot is cheaper, and Compute Savings Plans apply.
Amazon EKSA charge per cluster per hour, plus the EC2 instances, Fargate pods, or Auto Mode compute that run the pods.
Amazon ECRThe storage of the images, and data transfer.
  • Check the ECS, Fargate, EKS, and ECR pricing pages for the current prices.

Exam-Style Question

Scenario: A team needs to put a small containerized web application online with a load balancer, HTTPS, and auto scaling, with the least setup, as a new AWS customer. Which option should a solutions architect recommend?

  • A. Amazon EKS with self-managed nodes.
  • B. AWS App Runner.
  • C. Amazon ECS Express Mode.
  • D. ECS with the EC2 launch type and a manually configured load balancer.
Show Answer and Explanation

Correct answer: C. ECS Express Mode creates an ECS service on Fargate with a load balancer, scaling, and networking from a container image and two roles. App Runner is closed to new customers.

OptionResultReason
AIncorrectThis is the most work to set up and run.
BIncorrectApp Runner no longer accepts new customers.
CCorrectIt is AWS’s recommended simple path for container web applications.
DIncorrectIt needs servers and manual setup.

Exam Trap

Remember these points:

  • ECS has no extra charge. EKS charges per cluster per hour.
  • App Runner is closed to new customers. The current simple path is ECS Express Mode.

Memory Hook

Function: Lambda. Container, no servers: Fargate. Special hardware: EC2. Kubernetes: EKS.

8.2 Exam Scenarios

Scenario 1

Scenario: An image-processing service on ECS reads jobs from an SQS queue. The queue is empty at night and holds thousands of jobs during the day. The company wants no servers to manage and the lowest cost, and a job can be retried if it is interrupted.

Show Answer and Explanation

Answer: Run the service on Fargate, with a capacity provider strategy that favors Fargate Spot, and scale the number of tasks on the queue length with ECS Service Auto Scaling. The queue keeps the jobs safe if a Spot task is stopped.

Scenario 2

Scenario: Two ECS services run in the same cluster: one must write to an S3 bucket, and the other must read one DynamoDB table. The security team requires least privilege and no long-term credentials in the containers.

Show Answer and Explanation

Answer: Give each task definition its own task role, with only the S3 or DynamoDB permissions that the service needs. The containers get temporary credentials from the role, with no access keys.

Scenario 3

Scenario: A content management system runs as ECS tasks in three Availability Zones, and all tasks must read and write the same uploaded files, which must survive when tasks stop.

Show Answer and Explanation

Answer: Mount an Amazon EFS file system in the task definition. EFS is shared across Availability Zones and works with both the EC2 and Fargate launch types.

8.3 Lesson Summary

This lesson covered the following points:

  • Containers package an application with its dependencies and share the host kernel. ECS or EKS is the control plane, EC2 or Fargate is the data plane, and ECR stores the images.
  • ECR stores private and public images, with scanning, lifecycle policies, tag immutability, and replication.
  • In ECS, a task definition describes the containers, a task is a running copy, and a service keeps tasks running behind a load balancer. EventBridge can run standalone tasks.
  • The EC2 launch type gives control and special hardware. Fargate runs tasks without servers, with awsvpc networking, and Fargate Spot lowers the cost of interruptible work. Capacity providers mix them.
  • The task execution role serves ECS, and the task role serves the application. EFS gives shared storage, ALB routes to services, and Service Auto Scaling follows CPU, requests, or queues.
  • EKS runs managed Kubernetes, with Auto Mode, managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Fargate, or Hybrid Nodes, and EKS Pod Identity for permissions. ECS Anywhere and EKS Anywhere run containers on premises.
  • App Runner is closed to new customers, and ECS Express Mode is the recommended simple path.

Memory Hook

Store in ECR, orchestrate with ECS or EKS, run on EC2 or Fargate.

9. Knowledge Check

Answer each question in your own words before you open the model answer.

Question 1: Explain how containers differ from virtual machines, and the roles of ECR, ECS, EKS, EC2, and Fargate.

Maps to: Objective 1 (Comprehension).

A virtual machine runs its own guest operating system on a hypervisor, while containers share the host kernel, so they are smaller, start in seconds, and many run on one server. ECR stores the container images. ECS, the AWS orchestrator, and EKS, managed Kubernetes, are control planes that decide where containers run and keep them running. EC2 instances that you manage and Fargate, serverless compute, are the data planes that run the containers.

Question 2: Describe the ECR features that protect and manage images.

Maps to: Objective 2 (Application).

Repositories are private by default, with access controlled by IAM and repository policies, and images are encrypted at rest. Basic scanning checks images on push, and enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector to scan continuously. Lifecycle policies delete old or untagged images, tag immutability stops released tags from being overwritten, and replication copies images to other Regions or accounts.

Question 3: Explain task definitions, tasks, and services, and when to use a standalone task.

Maps to: Objective 3 (Application).

A task definition is the JSON blueprint of the containers: images, CPU and memory, ports, roles, network mode, and logging. A task is a running instance of it. A service keeps a desired number of tasks running, replaces failed ones, registers them with a load balancer, and rolls out new versions. A standalone task suits batch work that runs and stops, often started by an EventBridge schedule or event.

Question 4: Compare the EC2 and Fargate launch types, and explain when to use Fargate Spot.

Maps to: Objective 5 (Analysis).

With the EC2 launch type, you manage the instances, choose instance types including GPUs, pack tasks onto them, and pay for the instances. With Fargate, AWS runs each task without instances to manage, you choose CPU and memory per task, up to 16 vCPU and 120 GB, every task uses awsvpc networking, and you pay per second for what each task requests. Fargate Spot runs interruptible tasks at a lower price, with a two-minute warning before a stop, so it suits fault-tolerant work.

Question 5: Distinguish the task role and the task execution role, and describe how ECS services scale.

Maps to: Objective 4 (Application).

The task execution role lets ECS pull images from ECR, send logs to CloudWatch Logs, and read secrets for the task. The task role gives the application code its permissions to call AWS services, per task definition. ECS Service Auto Scaling uses Application Auto Scaling to change the number of tasks with target tracking on CPU, memory, or ALB requests, step scaling, or schedules, and worker services can scale on the length of an SQS queue. With EC2, an Auto Scaling group capacity provider adds instances.

Question 6: Explain when to choose EKS instead of ECS, and compare the EKS node types.

Maps to: Objective 6 (Evaluation).

Choose EKS when the team uses Kubernetes and its tools, needs portability across environments, or moves existing Kubernetes workloads, and choose ECS for a simpler AWS-native orchestrator with no control plane charge. In EKS, Auto Mode manages the nodes for you, managed node groups run EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group, self-managed nodes give full control, Fargate runs pods without nodes, and Hybrid Nodes add on-premises servers.

Question 7: Design the container platform for FlashCart: the catalog service with no servers to manage, behind a load balancer, with least-privilege access to DynamoDB, shared files, and scaling with the traffic.

Maps to: Objective 7 (Synthesis).

Store the images in private ECR repositories with enhanced scanning, lifecycle policies, and tag immutability. Run the catalog as an ECS service on Fargate across several Availability Zones, behind an Application Load Balancer with path-based routing. Give the task definition a task role that can read only the catalog table, a task execution role for ECR, logs, and secrets, and keep the passwords in Secrets Manager. Mount Amazon EFS for the shared files, scale the service with target tracking on CPU or the ALB request count, use Fargate Spot for interruptible jobs, and monitor with Container Insights.
